original_question: In the infinite-horizon Chow-Robbins fair-coin stopping game, a player repeatedly tosses a fair coin and may stop after any finite history with h heads and t tails, receiving the payoff h/(h+t) at the stopping time. The open problem is to determine the exact optimal stopping rule: for each state (h, t), decide rigorously whether stopping immediately is optimal or whether continuing yields a strictly larger expected payoff. In particular, the unresolved difficulty is proving that a given state is truly a STOP state rather than merely showing, by computation at some finite horizon, that continuing can be beneficial in other cases.
target_in_paper: The exact stopping rule, i.e. the decision whether to stop or go, is still an open problem for (infinitely) many cases.
correct_elements: The draft correctly describes the infinite-horizon fair-coin sequential stopping game with payoff h/(h+t) at stopping and identifies that the main open problem is to determine, for each state (h,t), whether stopping immediately is optimal (Section 1).
missing_details: Definition of the finite-horizon expected payoff f_N(h,t) via backward induction with boundary conditions (Equations (4.1)–(4.2)).
Existence of the limit F(h,t)=lim_{N→∞} f_N(h,t) (Equation (4.3)).
The decision criterion: stop if F(h,t)=h/(h+t), continue otherwise.
Clarification that F(h,t) is defined in terms of expectation and that proving STOP states requires rigorous upper bounds on f_N(h,t) valid for all N.
Specification of the state space (h,t)∈ℕ₀² and the assumption of a fair coin.
refined_question: Let (h,t)∈ℕ₀² denote the current counts of heads and tails in a sequential fair-coin tossing game. For each finite horizon N, define f_N(h,t) by the boundary condition f_N(h,N−h)=max{h/N,1/2} for 0≤h≤N and by backward induction f_N(h,t)=max{h/(h+t), (f_N(h+1,t)+f_N(h,t+1))/2} for h+t<N. Let F(h,t)=lim_{N→∞} f_N(h,t), which exists. The optimal stopping rule is: stop if F(h,t)=h/(h+t) and continue otherwise. The open problem is to determine exactly for which (h,t)∈ℕ₀² one has F(h,t)=h/(h+t)—equivalently, to rigorously characterize the stopping region S={ (h,t): F(h,t)=h/(h+t) } by proving, for each (h,t) in S, that h/(h+t)≥(f_N(h+1,t)+f_N(h,t+1))/2 holds for all N.
justification: We selected the statement of the open problem verbatim from Section 1, then incorporated the finite-horizon recursion, the existence of the infinite limit, and the precise stopping criterion from Section 4 to form a fully self-contained question that mirrors the paper’s original formulation.
